p.src: Last time we began asking how a charged particle moves in electric and magnetic fields once the principles of relativity are imposed. The familiar Lorentz force law already contains the clue: its magnetic term depends on the particle’s velocity, so different observers cannot agree separately about what is electric and what is magnetic. Our task is to formulate the law so that every inertial observer uses the same equation, even though the fields and the particle velocity change from frame to frame.

p.src: Electromagnetism and gravitation already warn us that relativistic extensions need not resemble one another. p.src:
Take two three-dimensional vectors $\boldsymbol A$ and $\boldsymbol B$. Their outer product $T_{mn}=A_mB_n$ is a rank-two tensor with nine components. It has no symmetry in general. Antisymmetrizing gives $K_{mn}=A_mB_n-A_nB_m,
  \qquad K_{mn}=-K_{nm}.$ Its diagonal entries vanish, while every entry below the diagonal is fixed by the corresponding entry above it. A $3\times3$ antisymmetric tensor therefore has only three independent components.

p.src:
The tensor notation makes the no-work property of a magnetic field nearly automatic. Differentiate the squared speed: $\begin{aligned}\frac{d}{dt}(v_mv_m)
  &=2\dot v_m v_m \\
  &\propto 2(\boldsymbol v\times\boldsymbol B)_m v_m \\
  &=2v_nB_{nm}v_m.
  \end{aligned}$ Terms with $m=n$ vanish because the diagonal of $B_{nm}$ is zero. Every off-diagonal term has a partner with $m$ and $n$ interchanged; the two cancel because $v_nv_m$ is symmetric while $B_{nm}$ is antisymmetric. Hence $\frac{d}{dt}(v_mv_m)=0.$ A pure magnetic force bends a trajectory without changing its speed or kinetic energy.

  &\propto 2(\boldsymbol v\times\boldsymbol B)_m v_m \\
  &=2v_nB_{nm}v_m.

p.src:
Because $p^\mu$ is a four-vector and $\tau$ a scalar, the natural relativistic left-hand side is $f^\mu\equiv\frac{dp^\mu}{d\tau}.$ The four-force cannot be chosen arbitrarily. Four-velocity has fixed norm, $u_\mu u^\mu=1.$ Differentiating along the world line gives $\begin{aligned}0
  &=\frac{d}{d\tau}(u_\mu u^\mu) \\
  &=\frac{du_\mu}{d\tau}u^\mu
    +u_\mu\frac{du^\mu}{d\tau} \\
  &=2u_\mu\frac{du^\mu}{d\tau}.\end{aligned}$ For constant mass this implies $f^\mu u_\mu=0.$ Thus four-force is Minkowski-orthogonal to four-velocity. This is a purely kinematic constraint following from the normalization of $u^\mu$, not a special property of electromagnetism.

For a boost along the $1$-axis, the coordinates transform as $\begin{aligned}x'^1&=\gamma(x^1-vx^0), &
  x'^0&=\gamma(x^0-vx^1), \\
  x'^2&=x^2, & x'^3&=x^3.\end{aligned}$ Apply the same transformation separately to both tensor indices. For the component parallel to the boost, the board begins with a product: $\begin{aligned}(A'^0B'^1)
  =\gamma^2\bigl(
     A^0B^1-vA^0B^0-vA^1B^1+v^2A^1B^0
   \bigr).\end{aligned}$ Replacing each product by the corresponding tensor component and then using antisymmetry, $F^{00}=F^{11}=0$ and $F^{10}=-F^{01}$, gives $F'^{01}
  =\gamma^2(1-v^2)F^{01}
  =F^{01}.$ Thus the electric field component parallel to the motion is unchanged. The parallel magnetic component behaves similarly.

A neutral current-carrying wire is therefore subtler than a single moving lump of charge. A purely magnetic field cannot be transformed completely away. We now leave the trajectory of one particle and consider a field throughout spacetime. Let $\phi=\phi(x^1,x^2,x^3,x^0)$ be a scalar field. Its four derivatives form the covariant components of a four-vector: $\partial_\mu\phi
  \equiv\frac{\partial\phi}{\partial x^\mu}
  =\left(
    \frac{\partial\phi}{\partial x},
    \frac{\partial\phi}{\partial y},
    \frac{\partial\phi}{\partial z},
    \frac{\partial\phi}{\partial t}
  \right).$ The chain rule applied to the Lorentz coordinate transformation proves this covariant transformation law. Raising the index reverses the spatial signs but leaves the time sign unchanged: $\partial^\mu\phi
  =\left(
    -\frac{\partial\phi}{\partial x},
    -\frac{\partial\phi}{\partial y},
    -\frac{\partial\phi}{\partial z},
    \frac{\partial\phi}{\partial t}
  \right).$
